newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korean defectors raise "boat people" fears.
newsitem.headline: North Korean defectors raise "boat people" fears.

text.p: South Koreans on Tuesday feared a mass influx of hungry North Korean "boat people" after two families aboard a wooden craft made possibly the first direct sea escape to the South.
The group of 14 defectors came ashore at the western port city of Inchon on a maritime police cutter after abandoning their boat on a remote island because of high waves.
Their daring four-day voyage, during which they mingled with the Chinese fishing fleet in the Yellow Sea to disguise their flight, set off alarm bells in the South.

South Koreans worry a collapse of the near-starving North could trigger a seaborne invasion of "boat people" similar to the Vietnamese refugees who landed on Asian shores in a flotilla of vessels starting in the 1970s.
"Is this a signal for a mass exodus by sea?" asked the Dong-A Ilbo newspaper.
"What has added shock is the fact that they are the first 'boat people' to defect to South Korea."

Doubts remain, however, about the account of the boat's captain Ahn Sun-kook, 48, who carried his mother on his back as he stepped ashore in pouring rain early on Tuesday. Ahn's wife, son and two daughters smiled brightly and waved to photographers.
A maritime police official said he had seen reports that a portable telephone, gas stove and South Korean-made cigarettes had been found on board the 32-tonne boat.

Since none of these luxury products are thought to be available in North Korea, there are suspicions the boat might have arrived via China, an increasingly common jumping-off point for North Korean asylum seekers.
Several newspapers also pointed out that North Korea is desperately short of fuel, and boats are not easily available, making mass flight by sea unlikely.

The boat carrying the two families of ordinary North Koreans was intercepted off the west coast of the Korean peninsula just south of a nautical demarcation line that has split the two Koreas since their 1950-53 war.

According to some media accounts it left a North Korean river port near China carrying the captain and his family and picked up the second family further down the coast before sailing for international waters.
"We came for freedom," said the boat's engineer Kim Won-hyung, 57, whose family of eight included his two year-old grandson who looked healthy and plump despite food shortages gripping the North.
"If the information provided by the captain is true, it would be the first defection direct by sea from North Korea," said Korea Maritime Police spokesman Chung Moo-chang.
They had outwitted North Korean naval patrol craft before being spotted by Southern naval radar on Monday.
Growing numbers of North Koreans are risking their lives in search of rice and a better life. All have escaped across the heavily-mined land border with the South or through China.
The largest mass escape was by a group of 17 -- including 16 members of a single family -- that arrived in the South last December after a six-week long epic escape through China and into Hong Kong.
Last month North Korea's former top ideologue, Hwang Jang-yop, arrived in Seoul after a flight through Beijing and the Philippines.
South Korea is preparing for a refugee crisis by building several reception centres near Seoul.
